title: Effect of silicon carbide (SiC) nanomaterials on the performance of the disc brake pads in vehicles: an experimental study
abstract: Abstract Composite materials are used in many industries, and one of the most important industries in which composite materials are used is the automobile industry. One of the parts whose performance depends most on composite materials in vehicles is the brake pads. The wear rate, friction rate, cooling rate, and overall brake performance depend on it. This study investigates the enhancement of brake pad performance by incorporating silicon carbide (SiC) nanoparticles as an abrasive additive. Testing was conducted on a specialized rig utilizing a standard grey cast iron ventilated disc (outer diameter of 241 mm and nominal thickness of 19 mm), consistent with the specifications of a 2005 Hyundai Excel. Four experimental formulations with SiC concentrations of 0, 0.5, 1.5, and 3 wt% were evaluated. The results demonstrate that the 0.5 wt% SiC concentration achieved the most significant improvement, increasing the average brake force by up to 19% and enhancing the friction coefficient compared to unmodified pads. Furthermore, the SiC-infused samples exhibited superior thermal stability and fade resistance at temperatures up to 130 °C, outperforming all other tested formulations and demonstrating more consistent reliability under different operating conditions.

title: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Poka-Yoke Support Hook for Brake Calipers During Brake Pad Replacement
journal: International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science
abstract: Temporarily supporting a removed brake caliper is a necessary part of brake maintenance because the hydraulic hose must not serve as a suspension element. This study examines the design of a caliper support hook made from AISI 1020 steel and interprets the graphical evidence from a static simulation. An applied case study was conducted, integrating a documentary review, an exploratory literature search guided by PRISMA transparency criteria, failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA), and interpretation of four numerical plots and one material data sheet. The model shown contains two hooks, perforated arms, joints, and a diagonal bar. The plot scales show upper limits of 36.56 MPa for von Mises equivalent stress, 0.1925 mm for resultant displacement, and 1.339 × 10⁻⁴ for equivalent strain. The visible distribution concentrates higher stress and strain near the upper-hook transition, while displacement increases toward the loaded lower end. The AISI 1020 data sheet indicates a yield strength of 351.571 MPa, consistent with the displayed minimum factor of safety of approximately 9.6. However, load, contact, and mesh-convergence documentation is missing, so no allowable capacity is established. title: System-Level Simulation of Air Disc Brake under Dynamic Braking Conditions for Design Optimization
journal: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
abstract: Air disc brakes are commonly used in trucks due to their superior performance compared to conventional drum brakes. To validate the brake assembly, extensive physical tests are conducted for the required brake torque condition. The aim of the study is to correlate the physical test deformation and failure modes using finite element analysis (FEA) and to optimize the design variables. Initially, there was a correlation gap between the test and FEA as the braking event was simulated with estimated static loads at the interfaces. Though the geometry is symmetric, during brake application, there are unsymmetric loads acting on the assembly along the direction of the rotation of the rotor due to dynamic deformation as the torque is generated at the friction pad interface. To simulate this unsymmetric behavior, the dynamic implicit analysis procedure with a moderate dissipation approach in Abaqus/Standard is used. title: Adaptive regenerative and friction braking torque allocation using deep reinforcement learning for electric vehicles
journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part D Journal of Automobile Engineering
abstract: The increasing adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) has accelerated the demand for intelligent regenerative braking strategies capable of improving braking energy recovery and reducing mechanical braking dependency under varying driving conditions. This paper proposes a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based personalized regenerative braking framework considering regenerative power limitation, battery state-of-charge (SOC) constraints, braking torque saturation, aerodynamic drag, rolling resistance, and emergency braking conditions. The proposed DRL controller adaptively allocates braking torque between regenerative and friction braking systems to maximize braking energy recovery while minimizing friction braking utilization. A reinforcement learning (RL)-based braking framework derived from existing literature is utilized as the baseline controller for comparative analysis. The proposed framework is implemented in MATLAB simulation environment under urban, city, and highway driving conditions using realistic EV parameters. The obtained results demonstrate that the proposed DRL framework significantly outperforms the RL-based controller. Regenerative braking energy recovery improvement varies from 106.77% to 185.60%, while friction braking reduction reaches up to 31.35%. In addition, the proposed framework improves battery SOC, brake pad operational life, and reduces brake service cost and particulate matter emissions under realistic electric vehicle operating conditions.

title: Influence of die face geometry on material flow, thermomechanical history, and microstructure in friction extrusion
abstract: Friction extrusion (FE) is a solid-phase process that can produce high-performance composites with homogeneous microstructures and low porosity via industrially scalable routes. However, the influence of die face geometry on material flow, thermomechanical history, and microstructure remains unclear. This work uses an experimentally validated smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) framework to quantify die-geometry effects during FE of AA1100 (O temper) rods for grid-conductor applications. Five dies are examined: flat (F), scrolled with (S-CB) and without (S) a counterbore, and conical scrolled with (CS-CB) and without (CS) a counterbore. The flat die exhibits a narrow sticking zone and pronounced slip near the orifice, leading to localized strain rate/temperature fields and strong core-edge gradients in plastic strain. Scrolls enlarge the effective processing zone and improve mixing by promoting interfacial sticking, whereas conical faces reduce contact pressure and homogenize thermomechanical fields. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) shows that CS and CS-CB yield the finest dynamically recrystallized grains. A Zener-Hollomon parameter-grain size relationship is further established, providing a physics‑based metric for FE die and process design.

title: Sliding a Helpless Adult Across a Bed: Friction, Sheet Materials, and the Pull One Caregiver Can Sustain
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: On a level bed, sliding a patient of 70 kg requires 274.7 N with a cotton sheet on a cotton mattress cover, 171.7 N with a cotton sheet on plastic sheeting, 103.0 N with a smooth synthetic sheet on plastic, and 54.9 N with a low-friction pair. For a patient of 90 kg the corresponding forces are 353.2 N, 220.7 N, 132.4 N, and 70.6 N. Against a stated sustained pull of 150 N for one caregiver, only the smooth synthetic sheet on plastic and the low-friction pair bring both the 70 kg and the 90 kg patient within one caregiver's sustained pull on the level. Sliding up an incline of 20 degrees raises every force sharply: even the low-friction pair requires 286.5 N for 70 kg. Controlling a downward slide on that incline with the low-friction pair requires a restraining force of 183.2 N for 70 kg.

title: FRICTIONAL CHARACTERISTICS OF A TRIBOSYSTEM WITH A COMBINED CONTACT SURFACE IN DRY AND BOUNDARY FRICTION MODES
abstract: The study objective is to determine the features of the contact interaction between the elements of a tribological pair with a combined contact surface under dry and boundary friction conditions. The task the paper is devoted to is assessing the influence of sliding velocity and lubricant on the friction characteristics of a friction system with a combined surface “structural steel – deposited metal”, simulating the contact between the working edge of a tool and a combined machinable material. Research methods. The friction characteristics are assessed using the “indenter on disc” friction scheme, with the sliding velocity varied both in a dry state and with the use of commercial lubricating and cooling fluids. The indenter materials are hard alloy T15K6 and high speed steel R18; the combined disc surface consists of structural steel 09G2S and metal deposited with an electrode. During the experiments, the values of the friction coefficients were recorded. Novelty of the work. The influence of sliding velocity and lubricant on changes in the friction factor when passing through material separation boundaries for a tribosystem with a combined contact surface is revealed. Research results. title: Efficient Simulation of the Form-Based Manufacturing of Friction-Spun Joint Connectors
journal: OPUS FAU (Kooperativer Bibliotheksverbund Berlin-Brandenburg (KOBV), on behalf of the Universitätsbibliothek Erlangen-Nürnberg)
abstract: Friction-spun joint connectors (FSJC) are a highly versatile joining process for tackling the challenges posed by multi-material systems. The process allows for adapting the joining element inline to the requirements and can process a variety of materials. Recently, the potential of a form-based manufacturing approach for FSJC was demonstrated. Herein, a suitable simulation approach is presented that targets an improved process understanding to eventually tailor the forming and to reduce wear. A 3D modelling approach would be challenging due to the high-speed rotation, large deformations, frictional contact, and discretization requirements. A standard 2D model, however, lacks the angular velocity, which generates the heat during friction spinning. Therefore, an efficient 2D axisymmetric substitution model is proposed, which mimics the frictional heat generation. This allows for simulating and investigating the form-based manufacturing of FSJC. A qualitative agreement to experimental results is achieved, but for a predictive simulation, further investigations into the mechanical, thermal, and frictional behaviour of the processed materials are necessary to capture the wide temperature range.

title: Effect of Bio-Inspired Surface Textures On Friction and Wear Under Solid-Lubricated Conditions
abstract: Abstract Surface texturing offers a promising approach for improving tribological performance; however, systematic comparisons of different bio-inspired texture architectures under solid-lubricated conditions remain limited. This study investigates the tribological behaviour of conventional dimple and bio-inspired honeycomb and snakeskin textures fabricated on tungsten carbide pins using laser machining. Pin-on-disc experiments were conducted against AA6061 discs under MoS2-grease-based solid lubrication at rotational speeds of 250 and 1250 rpm. The coefficient of friction (COF), post-test mass variation, wear depth, wear cross-sectional area, and surface morphology were evaluated, while SEM and EDS analyses characterized material transfer and surface evolution. At 250 rpm, the dimple, honeycomb, and snakeskin textures reduced the COF by approximately 36%, 41%, and 59%, respectively, compared with the plain pin. At 1250 rpm, the corresponding reductions were approximately 51%, 51%, and 53%. The snakeskin texture exhibited the lowest COF, wear depth, and wear cross-sectional area at both rotational speeds. The dimple texture exhibited the highest pin mass gain and the lowest net disc mass loss among textured conditions, accompanied by greater accumulation of Al adhered material within its cavities. title: Current-Carrying Friction Behavior and Interfacial Evolution Mechanism of Copper Alloys for Industrial Chromium-Plating Cathodes
abstract: In sliding electrical contact processes, the effects of applied electric current on frictional behavior and surface damage are not aligned, and elucidating the relationship between the two is critical for optimizing the performance of conductive friction pairs in continuous chromium plating systems. In this study, reciprocating friction tests on a self-lubricating copper alloy were performed under varying normal loads (5–20 N) and applied currents (0–5 A), and the frictional response and interfacial evolution of the material were characterized via 3D profilometry, SEM, EDS, and XRD. The results demonstrate that under a 10 N load, the applied current generally reduces the friction coefficient, while the wear-track volume exhibits a non-monotonic trend with current variation. Microstructural analysis reveals that current-carrying friction is accompanied by plastic flow of the Cu matrix, redistribution of carbon-enriched regions, and enhanced surface oxygen signals, reflecting dynamic interfacial evolution under the combined action of mechanical shear and electric current. This work uncovers the asynchronous relationship between current-carrying friction reduction and surface damage evolution, providing experimental evidence for operating condition optimization of sliding conductive materials in continuous chromium plating systems.

title: Traveling-wave ultrasonic motors: reconciling friction and wear through structural-interfacial engineering
abstract: Abstract Unlike conventional electromagnetic motors, traveling-wave ultrasonic motors (TWUMs) offer high torque density, low noise, simple construction, and inherent self-locking. Despite these advantages, their industrial adoption remains limited by a persistent lack of integrated optimization strategies that simultaneously balance multiple performance metrics. This review systematically evaluates recent advances in TRUMs from three interconnected perspectives: stator/rotor architecture, contact-interface tribology, and novel operating principles. We identify critical gaps — particularly in wear control under ultrasonic vibration, multi-physics coupling (mechanical–thermal–electrical–acoustic), and the temperature stability of lead-free piezoelectric ceramics such as KNN-based materials. Notably, surface micro-texturing with optimized parameters increases the friction coefficient by up to 36.3% and reduces adhesive wear. Structural modifications — including embedded piezoelectric stacks, double-sided staggered teeth, and suspended stators — substantially improve no-load speed and stall torque. Non-contact designs eliminate mechanical wear but currently deliver limited torque (<50 mN·m), confining them to precision rather than power applications. We propose a three-level optimization framework — structural, interfacial, and operational — that unifies previously fragmented efforts. title: Determination of Pavement Marking Friction Levels and an Equivalent Wear Model Correlating Laboratory Polishing with Field Traffic Conditions
journal: Journal of Transportation Engineering Part B Pavements
abstract: Abstract Pavement marking friction is a critical factor in roadway safety, especially for vulnerable users such as pedestrians, bicyclists, and motorcyclists. However, standardized testing procedures and performance criteria remain undeveloped in the United States. The absence of a laboratory-to-field polishing equivalency relationship further hinders this process. To address these gaps, this study correlates laboratory polishing with field traffic conditions by establishing a systematic friction-level classification and developing an equivalent wear model. Building upon prior research, this work examines the friction performance of 23 pavement marking-additive combinations, encompassing six marking materials, three glass bead sizes, ceramic particles, and three antiskid particle sizes. Friction is measured by the British Pendulum Tester (BPT) and the dynamic friction tester (DFT), with simulated wear applied using the three-wheel polishing device (TWPD). Based on the Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) clustering analysis and engineering interpretation, three British Pendulum Number (BPN) levels are defined: 35 ≤ BPN < 45 (Level 1), 45 ≤ BPN < 60 (Level 2), and BPN ≥ 60 (Level 3). Corresponding dynamic friction (DF40) thresholds are determined through spline-based interpolation to provide cross-reference values for agencies or studies that use DFT-based friction measurements. title: Study on the Current Carrying Friction and Wear Performance of Conductive Rollers for Ni-Cr Electroplating at High Current Density
abstract: Conductive rollers in Ni-Cr electroplating require wear-resistant surfaces under current-carrying contact. Ag coatings are susceptible to deformation and wear, while the protective response of Ag-Cu coatings under lubricated current-carrying sliding remains insufficiently characterized. In this study, an Ag-Cu coating was prepared on a T2 Cu substrate by rotary spray deposition and evaluated through microstructural characterization, nanoindentation, and sliding tests. Current-carrying friction tests were conducted at 20 N under PAO 10 lubrication for 30 min. The coating exhibited a higher mean hardness (1.943 ± 0.997 GPa vs. 1.055 ± 0.070 GPa) than the substrate. At 20 A, the coating maintained a coefficient of friction of approximately 0.12 and exhibited a wear volume of 2.44 × 10−3 mm3 within the measured region, 19.7% lower than that of the substrate. Morphological and elemental observations were consistent with oxidation and material redistribution. No clear overall advantage was observed at 10 A, whereas severe damage occurred at 30 A despite lower friction. These results indicate a protective benefit at 20 A under the tested conditions and support further evaluation of Ag-Cu coatings for conductive roller protection.

title: ADVANCEMENTS IN FRICTION STIR WELDING OF DISSIMILAR LIGHTWEIGHT ALLOYS: MICROSTRUCTURAL EVOLUTION, MECHANICAL PERFORMANCE, AND INTERFACE STRENGTHENING
journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MECHANICAL ENGINEERING AND TECHNOLOGY (IJMET)
abstract: The escalating demand for lightweight structural components in the automotive, aerospace, petrochemical, oil & gas and marine sectors has intensified the need for robust joining technologies capable of integrating dissimilar lightweight alloys without the metallurgical penalties associated with fusion-based processes.Friction stir welding (FSW), a solid-state joining technique operating below the melting temperature of the base materials, has emerged as a premier solution for overcoming the inherent challenges of dissimilar alloy combinations such as Al/Mg, Al/Ti, and Al/Cu.This paper presents a comprehensive critical review of recent advancements in the FSW of dissimilar lightweight alloys, with a focused examination of microstructural evolution, mechanical performance, and interface strengthening mechanisms.The analysis reveals that the thermo-mechanical cycle intrinsic to FSW promotes dynamic recrystallization, yielding refined equiaxed grain structures within the stir zone, while simultaneously driving the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds (IMCs) at the dissimilar interface. title: Quantifying the Roles of Yarn–Yarn Interfacial Stiffness and Friction in Load Transfer of Plain-Woven Kevlar 49 Fabrics
abstract: Micro-Raman spectroscopy offers an optical, non-contact route to stress metrology in fibrous materials: the Raman peak of aramid fiber shifts linearly with axial strain, so the spectral signal acquired at a laser-probed point directly reflects the local stress state. Here, Raman spectra of Kevlar 49 plain-woven fabrics were acquired with a 785 nm laser at 10 mW through a 10× objective over 1540–1650 cm−1, and the G′ band was tracked point by point along a drawn warp yarn to build spatially resolved stress profiles under drawing loads of 3–9 N and transverse preloads of 0 and 30 N. The optically measured profiles were inverted, through a two-zone friction–adhesion model, into interfacial shear parameters and a stress-transfer coefficient, and then analyzed via sensitivity analysis. The spectra show that transverse preload raises the effective sliding-friction shear stress by 57–78% and the maximum static interfacial shear stress by 60–75%. Sensitivity analysis shows that yarn–yarn interfacial stiffness governs the spatial decay of stress far more strongly than yarn elastic modulus, and defines a characteristic load transfer length. This spectral-shift-to-mechanics framework links optical measurements to interfacial design of high-performance fabrics.

title: Microstructure, mechanical properties and corrosion resistance of underwater friction stir welded dissimilar joints of AA6061 and AA7075 aluminium alloys
abstract: This work investigated the effects of process parameters on the microstructural and mechanical properties of dissimilar aluminium alloys AA7075 and AA6061 by the underwater Friction stir welding process. The welding of dissimilar alloys is crucial for aerospace and structural applications due to their distinct mechanical properties. Rapid heat dissipation can mitigate the effects of heat in dissimilar aluminium alloy welding. So, the advanced technique of FSW, i.e., underwater friction stir welding (UFSW), has significant capacity to weld soft and dissimilar alloys without cracks, with lower residual stresses, and with improved strength. However, the present study is an attempt to evaluate the performance of UFSWed joints at different tool rotational speeds (TRS) from 600 rpm to 1400 rpm and transverse welding speeds (WS) from 15 mm/min to 60 mm/min. The combination of these two considered process parameters is made because they can significantly affect heat generation. The study revealed that the UFSW of AA6061-AA7075 joints achieved an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of approximately 78.41% of the base material, AA6061, at 1000 rpm and 35 mm/min, with an elongation of 7.1%. The hardness values of all welded joints drop rapidly to around 82-100 HV as the indentation path approaches the TMAZ.

title: Identification of Friction and Wear Regimes in Tribosystems Using Acoustic Emission: Dissipation Criterion, Metallographic Analysis, and Life Prediction Model
abstract: Abstract A methodology integrating acoustic emission (AE) power parameters, metallographic analysis, Fourier sub-block orientation analysis, and EDS mapping is developed for the identification of quasi-wearless friction regimes in tribosystems. A dimensionless dissipation coefficient ξ TC = µ*·W*/W L × 100% is introduced as a unified thermodynamic criterion separating Mode I (equilibrium self-organisation, ξ TC = 0.0836–0.0941%) from Mode II (non-equilibrium self-organisation, ξ TC = 6.86×10⁻⁴–6.94×10⁻⁴%). Three tribosystems are investigated over 36 controlled experiments: 12Kh2N4A steel disc–disc under boundary lubrication B3V (Б3В), VB23NTs bronze–30Kh3VA steel pair, and 30Kh3VA steel with PVD MoN–TiAlN coatings under ТС-1 lubricant. The life-prediction model's primary validated result is obtained for the PVD-coated Tribosystem C (R² = 0.992, mean error 3.4%, genuine blind hold-out verification on 17 independent experiments: 7 for calibration, 10 withheld); consistent Mode II regressions independently derived for Tribosystems A and B (R² = 0.992 for both, three experiments each, evaluated in-sample) corroborate the model across two further, structurally distinct material systems, though these smaller-sample fits should be regarded as preliminary. title: A Self-Burrowing Percussive Mole for Subsurface Thermal Measurements on Mars Sized from Hammer-Energy and Friction Bounds
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This paper presents the sizing of a surface system for Mars, designed around a single operating principle and computed from published material properties of its working environment. The headline results are: advance per blow of 0.08 mm; advance rate in 8 h of operation of 3.456 m/day; time to 5 m of 1.447 days. Every figure was produced by the accompanying computation script from stated assumptions about density, strength, thermal properties and composition; no figure is asserted without its derivation. This study is a computation, not a measurement: the design is SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED, and no hardware has been built or tested.

title: A Slip Bound for Sole Materials on Wet Hillside Surfaces
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Wet slopes are where inexpensive soles fail most dangerously, yet sole choice for hillside work is usually made by habit. This paper computes a slip bound for five sole materials — smooth leather, flat rubber, lugged tyre tread, wood, and rope or coir — on four wet surfaces — wet rock, wet clay, mud, and wet wood — using stated friction coefficients. A combination slips at a slope angle of arctan(μ), and a safe working angle applies a safety factor of 1.5 to friction, giving arctan(μ/1.5). Taking a stated safe working slope of 20 degrees for hillside paths and farm terraces, the required coefficient is 0.3640 without any safety factor and 0.5460 with the factor applied. The result is stark: only 7 of the 20 combinations reach even the bare 20-degree threshold, and none of the 20 reaches 20 degrees with the safety factor — the best combination in the set, lugged tyre tread on wet clay (μ = 0.50), has a slip angle of 26.57 degrees but a safe working angle of only 18.43 degrees. The worst common combination, smooth leather on mud (μ = 0.12), slips at 6.84 degrees and is safe, on this criterion, only to 4.57 degrees. title: Analysis of the mechanical properties of additively manufactured matrix materialed Item
abstract: Friction stir additive manufacturing (FSAM) is an emerging solid-state process that adapts the principles of friction stir welding to fabricate aluminium components in a layer-by-layer manner. This study systematically investigates the mechanical properties, microstructural evolution, fracture behaviour, and phase composition of FSAM-fabricated aluminium specimens, benchmarked against conventional base materials AA 1050-H14 and AA 6082-T6. The evaluation incorporates tensile testing, hardness measurements, flexural behaviour, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to establish a comprehensive understanding of FSAM’s feasibility for structural applications.Tensile testing revealed position-dependent variations in FSAM specimens, with fractures predominantly occurring at the thermo-mechanically affected zone (TMAZ) and TMAZ–stir zone (SZ) interface, except at the end position (FSAM-E), which exhibited improved ductility in the heat-affected zone (HAZ). While the ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of FSAM specimens was consistently lower than that of AA 6082, strength increased progressively towards the end of the build, reflecting improved interlayer bonding and process stability. title: Cross-Project Relationships and Preliminary Estimation of Duncan–Chang E-B Parameters for Rockfill Materials
abstract: Reliable selection of Duncan–Chang E-B parameters for rockfill materials commonly relies on large-scale triaxial testing, which may be incomplete during preliminary investigations. This study examines cross-project transferability using 191 database test records from 35 dam projects. Material characteristics and engineering classifications were assessed by correlation analysis, mutual information, and held-out project permutation importance. Random forest regression estimated the initial tangent modulus coefficient, bulk modulus coefficient, and reference friction angle; other parameters were represented by shrinkage-adjusted group statistics or empirical ranges. Five-fold validation, with entire projects held out in each fold, and leave-one-project-out validation assessed generalization to unseen projects. With numerical and engineering classification descriptors combined, five-fold coefficients of determination (R2, with one indicating perfect agreement with the reference values) were 0.2992, 0.1907, and 0.3885 for the three directly estimated parameters, respectively. Under five-fold validation, adding engineering classifications to the numerical descriptors reduced pooled normalized mean absolute errors in initial tangent and bulk stiffness responses by 8.59% and 6.84%, respectively. title: The Dynamic Periodic Table of Matter: A Generative Recursive Framework for Background-Free, Adaptive Electrodynamic Systems and Material Phases
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Traditional physics and materials science have long been anchored in a "substance ontology" and background-dependent continuous space-time (relying on an external clock of "God ticking seconds"), treating macroscopic resistance as a fixed parameter. To overcome this paradigm bottleneck, this paper establishes a background-free, adaptive generative discrete recursive framework based on computational ontology. By introducing two core axioms—endogenous time (n) and continued fraction gear geometry (pnqn replacing )—we demonstrate that dynamic evolution is the sole reality, whereas static states are merely degenerate special cases. Crucially, we prove that macroscopic impedance and dissipation are not meaningless frictional costs, but rather topological mismatch residuals (n) acting as the "anchor of existence" that grounds matter in reality. Furthermore, we unify six classic material classes (from normal conductors to superconductors and phase-change materials) as different adaptive "UI rendering skins" of the same underlying recursive engine. This framework smoothly degrades to classical continuous limits while predicting micro-periodic resonance glitches under ultra-precision measurements, opening a new generative epoch for material science. title: Silicone, Thermoplastic Elastomer, and Polyurethane Prosthetic Liners: Material-Dependent Biomechanics, Clinical Decision-Making, and Research Priorities - A Critical Narrative Review
journal: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)
abstract: Background: Prosthetic liners couple soft residual-limb tissues to a comparatively rigid socket. Their mechanical response may modify loading and suspension, while limited heat and vapor transfer can complicate prolonged wear. Material-family labels are often used in prescription despite marked product-to-product variation. Objective: To examine what published comparisons actually establish about silicone, thermoplastic elastomer (TPE), and polyurethane (PU) liners, and to distinguish measurable material differences from unproven clinical assumptions. Methods: This critical narrative review integrates selected peer-reviewed investigations of liner compression, shear, tension, friction, and thermal conductivity. Evidence is organized by test domain and clinical relevance. Because no exhaustive database screening or formal risk-of-bias procedure was completed, the synthesis is not described as systematic. Findings: In one commercial-product comparison, mean compressive tangent moduli were 310 ± 100 kPa for silicone, 140 ± 30 kPa for TPE, and 300 ± 40 kPa for PU; corresponding shear values were 69 ± 17, 21 ± 5, and 63 ± 3 kPa. Reinforcement strongly affected tensile response, and tested PU products had comparatively low friction. These results describe particular products and protocols, not intrinsic polymer constants or demonstrated patient-outcome advantages. title: Metal Ions Immobilization and Strength Behaviour of Coal Mine Overburden Waste Materials Treated with Microbial Induced Calcite Precipitate Technique – Experimental and DEM Analyses
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Coal Mine Overburden Waste (CMOW) material in the coal mining industry possesses serious environmental risk through the leaching of hazardous and toxic heavy metals along with geotechnical constraints because of the low strength. Hence, the primary objective of the present study is to examine the efficacy of Microbially Induced Calcite Precipitation (MICP) technique to immobilize the metal ions present in the CMOW and simultaneously to investigate the enhancement in the Unconfined Compressive Strength (UCS). title: Active fluid patterning in inhomogeneous environments
abstract: Active stresses in biological cells and tissues drive many developmental processes. However, increasing experimental evidence suggests that additional mechanical interactions with surrounding material can play a crucial role in guiding these processes. We introduce a minimal model of this scenario and investigate how pattern formation in an active material can be controlled by an inhomogeneous environment. Specifically, we consider an active fluid in which a chemical species regulates local active stresses and is redistributed by the resulting flows. We show that active stress patterns within such a fluid exhibit frictiotaxis and systematically characterize how inhomogeneous external friction affects mechanochemical pattern formation instabilities. We find that hydrodynamic screening plays a crucial role in mediating the cross-talk between friction patterns and active fluid self-organization and identify a mechanochemical frustration mechanism that gives rise to pattern oscillations caused by inhomogeneous friction.

title: Recent advances in lubrication mechanisms of electrospun nanofibers: Oil-mediated and non-oil strategies
abstract: Abstract Friction and wear develop inherently at the dynamic interfaces of moving devices, leading to considerable energy losses and shortened lifespans. To overcome these challenges beyond conventional methods, precise structural control of the contact interface is essential, and developing tailored lubricating structures is therefore imperative for modern machinery. By exploiting the high specific surface area, aspect ratio, and porosity, together with the interconnected three-dimensional network structure of electrospun nanofibers, this review discusses the effects of surface morphology on lubricant behavior. Low-friction systems based on electrospun nanofibers are classified as oil-mediated self-lubricating nanofibers and non-oil interfacial and structural low-friction nanofibers. In oil-mediated systems, core-shell nanofibers store and release liquid lubricants from their internal cores, whereas non-core-shell nanofiber networks retain and structure oil to maintain an oil-rich lubricating environment. In addition, the friction reduction mechanisms are analyzed by focusing on lubricant storage and release, oil structuring, formation of hydration- and ion-based interfacial lubrication layers, reduction of interfacial shear resistance by solid lubricants, and the mechanical load-bearing effect of the nanofiber network. This review summarizes how nanofiber structure and material composition govern the friction and wear behavior of these systems.

title: Adaptive Technological Processes for Urban Road Network Maintenance in Mountainous Terrain: Mathematical Modeling and Hydrochemical Verification
abstract: Non-exhaust particulate emissions from road dust represent a major air-quality concern in mountain-basin cities, where restricted atmospheric dispersion promotes pollutant accumulation. This study develops an adaptive framework for urban road maintenance that integrates road-dust resuspension modelling, a nonlinear model of pavement friction response to de-icing material dosage, computational fluid dynamics analysis of street-canyon effects, and snow-cover hydrochemical monitoring. Field sampling was conducted at eight road sites and one background site in Almaty, Kazakhstan, during three campaigns in the 2024–2025 winter season. Meltwater pH, turbidity, and color were measured and incorporated into a diagnostic index for identifying road sections requiring maintenance adjustments. The measured pH ranged from 5.5 to 9.3, while January turbidity reached 68 mg/L at the most polluted site. The modelling results indicated that the principal improvement in pavement friction occurred within a de-icing material dosage range of 40–60 g/m2, whereas further dosage increases produced limited additional friction benefits. Scenario calculations suggested that adaptive dosing and the replacement of mechanical sweeping with vacuum or hydrodynamic cleaning at high-resuspension sites could reduce material consumption by 20–30% and potentially decrease road-dust resuspension by 30–50%. title: Nonsmooth Contact Dynamics for Flexible Multibody Systems with Ball Bearings
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Many machines and mechanisms operate under severe dynamic conditions involving high-speed rotations, frictional contact and multiple impacts. In this context, computational simulation is a useful tool for evaluating configurations, materials and operating conditions before prototype construction. The main contribution of this work is the development, the implementation and the validation of numerical models for complex mechanical systems with ball-bearing joints subjected to impacts within the framework of nonsmooth contact dynamics. The motion of rigid and flexible bodies is described by a nonlinear finite-element formulation, and contact with friction is treated through an augmented Lagrangian approach. The equations of motion are integrated with the decoupled nonsmooth generalized-alpha scheme, while contact-force histories are recovered by combining the impulses and velocity jumps obtained from the nonsmooth formulation with local smooth-contact laws.

abstract: This study revalidates retention robustness for one canonical closed pose of the 16-DoF LEAP Hand in the NVIDIA Isaac Lab. title: Regolith Flow and Bearing on Asteroid Ryugu: Slope, Settling and Contact Budgets at 120 Micro-g
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Ryugu's surface gravity of about 1.200e-04 metres per second squared places its regolith in a regime where a hopping lander's contact pressure rivals the soil's bearing strength. With density 1,190.0 kg per cubic metre, adopted cohesion 1 Pa and friction angle 35 degrees, the bearing capacity is 46.596 Pa, of which the gravity term supplies only 0.4755 Pa. Against a hopper contact pressure of 2 Pa the margin is 23.298. Granular flow over a 10 m slope moves at a scale of 0.0346 metres per second and disturbed material takes about 288.7 seconds to settle, while the body's spin period of 7.63 hours sits far from the critical 3.026 hours at which its equator would shed material.

title: Effect of electromagnetic coupling treatment on the tribological properties of YG6X hard metal
abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the effect of electromagnetic coupling treatment on YG6X cemented carbide by comparing the phase composition, mechanical properties (especially hardness) and tribological properties of untreated samples, single-pulse magnetic field-treated samples and magnetic-electric field coupling-treated samples, so as to provide technical support for the high-performance development and application expansion of cemented carbides. Design/methodology/approach This study uses YG6X cemented carbide as the sample, designing three groups: Untreated (0 V, 0 T), Craft1 (single-pulse magnetic field, 0 V, 1.5 T) and Craft2 (electromagnetic coupling, 1.5 V, 1.5 T). Samples are polished and ultrasonically cleaned. XRD analyzes phase composition, a microhardness tester measures hardness and a friction tester conducts dry reciprocating sliding tests. 3D profilometer, SEM and EDS are used to observe wear morphology and element distribution. Findings This study finds that electromagnetic coupling treatment (Craft2) outperforms untreated and single-pulse magnetic field treatment (Craft1) on YG6X cemented carbide. It promotes WC and Co3O4 phase formation, reduces internal stress and increases hardness by approximately 6%. title: Tribology of TiNbCr MPEA: Insights into tribolayer formation and resulting wear resistance
journal: Journal of materials research/Pratt's guide to venture capital sources
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the tribological behavior of the equiatomic TiNbCr multi-principal element alloy (MPEA), focusing on the role of phase constitution and microstructural heterogeneity in wear performance. The alloy exhibits a microstructure composed of a Nb- and Ti-rich BCC matrix and a Cr-rich C15 Laves phase, resulting in high hardness (~ 466 HV 0.5 ) and a relatively low elastic modulus (115 ± 4 GPA). Tribological tests reveal wear behavior dependence on the counter-body material Al 2 O 3 or Si 3 N 4 . Against Si 3 N 4 , the alloy shows superior wear resistance despite higher friction ( µ ≈ 0.7), which may be associated with the formation of a Si-containing tribolayer and the high hardness of the TiNbCr substrate. In contrast, sliding against Al 2 O 3 promotes unstable tribolayer formation, leading to material removal due to adhesive interaction and material transfer. These findings demonstrate that dry sliding wear resistance in TiNbCr MPEAs is governed by intrinsic mechanical properties and by tribochemical reactions.

title: Lubricate, Degrade, and Fertilize: A Multifunctional Superlubricating Hydrogel Inspired by Dolphin Skin
abstract: Abstract Engineering materials generally face challenges in simultaneously achieving high load-bearing capacity, superlubricity, and biodegradability. Additionally, they may impose an environmental burden upon disposal. Inspired by the microstructure of dolphin skin, this study developed a multifunctional superlubricating hydrogel composed of yam extract-PEGDA. It also proposed a dual-mechanism model in which micron-scale pore structures and hydration layer induced by hydrogen bonding synergistically contribute to the superlubricating performance. The hydrogel exhibits instantaneous superhydrophilicity, with a friction coefficient as low as 0.00191 under a contact pressure of 1.368 MPa. After 180 min of operation, the volumetric efficiency of the water hydraulic circular gear pump dropped to 58.3% with the uncoated bearing but remained at 82.7% with the hydrogel-coated bearing. After 30 days of soil incubation, the hydrogel showed ∼15.1% mass loss. Moreover, 14-day cultivation showed that soil with degraded hydrogel increased lettuce dry weight by ∼126.3% compared to the control group. This material combines the potential for sustained water-based lubrication with degradation-induced soil fertilization, providing a new strategy for developing green biomimetic lubricating materials.

title: Laser Treatment of Al Parts Used for Engines by Surface Alloying with Fe Powder
abstract: The combustion engine elements of automobiles are often built from aluminium alloy pistons that slide against cylinders made of cast iron with oil lubrication. For reducing friction and preventing scuffing between pistons and the cylinder, the pistons are sometimes coated. Another possibility is to create a specially treated surface layer, using ceramic particles and laser technology. Using a laser beam makes it possible to locally melt the surface of a piston and incorporate ceramic particles into the molten material. Since ceramic particles are significantly harder than aluminium alloys, this laser-based technology enhances a piston’s resistance to abrasive wear. Furthermore, a laser can be used to create microscopic indentations on the piston surface. This increased roughness helps retain an oil film, which improves lubrication and reduces the risk of dry friction and engine seizure. For this reason, in this work the influence of fibre laser processing parameters on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the aluminium–silicon alloy, especially the crystallographic structure changes, were studied. For alloying, iron powder was used with a size of approximately 60 µm. For investigation of the crystallographic structure, electron diffraction was used on the transmission electron microscope. title: Apollo Regolith Compaction with Depth: Density, Porosity and Overburden Budgets from the Lunar Surface Down
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Lunar regolith compacts under its own weight into a profile that every surface operation must work through. Adopting the Apollo-era density model, rising from 1,300.0 kg per cubic metre at the surface toward 1920 kg per cubic metre at depth with a scale depth of 0.15 m, this paper computes density and porosity at six depths, the overburden stress at 0.6 m, and a strip-footing bearing capacity for the compacted material. Porosity falls from 0.5240 at 5 cm to 0.3809 at 1 m. The overburden at 0.6 m is only 1,718.3 Pa, yet the bearing capacity reaches 3.884e+04 Pa, a margin of 8.264 over a lunar-module-class footpad pressure, because cohesion and friction, not weight, carry the load.

title: Abrasive Wear of HH Heat-Resistant Stainless Steels Used in Pelletizing Furnace Grate Bars
abstract: The abrasive wear of A297-HH heat-resistant stainless steel casting grate bars used to transport iron ore pellets in pelletizing furnaces was investigated. The grate bars operate under severe conditions, experiencing high temperatures and wear due to contact with the pellets. Microstructural analyses via metallography and Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS) identified chromium carbides (Cr23C6) and austenite, consistent with predictions from Thermo-Calc® software. Linear scratch tests were carried out using diamond and synthetic hematite Rockwell C indenters, applying progressive normal loads ranging from 0.2 to 10 N. Pin-on-disc wear tests were also performed to evaluate the tribological performance, using a synthetic hematite counter body to simulate real-world operating conditions. The predominant wear micromechanisms included micro-gouging and micro-cutting, with coefficients of friction ranging from 0.65 to 0.68 in the pin-on-disc tests. At 150°C in the pin-on-disc test, no mass loss was observed; instead, material transfer resulted in mass gain. The increase in microhardness in the wear tracks indicated surface work hardening. The results provide insights into wear mechanisms and material performance under different conditions, contributing to improved material selection and operational strategies.

title: Crushed Brick Waste–Soil Mixtures for Embankment Applications: A Bimsoil Characterization Using Large-Scale Multistage Shear Tests and Technical Applications
abstract: Crushed brick waste (CBW) is a major fraction of construction and demolition waste, yet design-oriented shear strength data for its reuse in earthworks remain scarce. This study examines CBW–soil mixtures within the block-in-matrix soil (Bimsoil) framework and quantifies their shear strength at large scale. The block-to-matrix contrast was checked through elastic modulus, friction angle, and unconfined compressive strength ratios. Large-scale multistage direct shear tests with a double shear-plane configuration were performed on one specimen per mixture, with the volumetric block proportion (VBP) ranging from 0% to 67%, and the failure point of every stage was defined with a single strain-based criterion. The friction angle increased from 21.3° to 38.3° with VBP, following a significant linear trend (R2 = 0.94), whereas the apparent cohesion dropped from 29.1 kPa for the natural soil to 10.6–18.5 kPa for the mixtures, without a significant trend among them. For VBP ≥ 48%, the envelopes intersect that of the natural soil at 46–52 kPa, within the tested range, so the natural soil governs at lower and the mixtures at higher normal stresses. In illustrative 6 m high gabion- and geogrid-reinforced soil walls, VBP of 67% reduced the gabion weight and geogrid area by 44.4% and 59.1% and by 28–45% and 19–61% over the examined wall heights and surcharges. These results provide a material-specific basis for selecting CBW content in embankments and retaining-wall backfills.

title: MUSEALIZAÇÃO ENTRE CADEIAS: OBJETOS APREENDIDOS E DOCUMENTAÇÃO NO ACERVO NO MPERJ
abstract: This article analyzes the tensions between the penal disciplinary apparatus and the musealization process. Exploring the friction between the concept of "musealization chain" and the materiality of the imprisonment "chain," this text problematizes the collection, documentation and exhibition of prison artifacts at the Rio de Janeiro State Penitentiary Museum (MPERJ), especially focusing on how seized illicit objects mimic the surveillance logic of institutions of sequestration. It argues that traditional museographic practice, driven by an Apollonian ordering vocation, neutralizes the transgressive urgency of these objects. By displacing them from the prison environment to the MPERJ, their musealization can act as a subsequent symbolic imprisonment, converting polysemic products into controlled information units. The paper concludes that, in order not to act as a reinforcement annex of the State punishment system, the museum must understand the complexity of inserting such objects into its operational chain, so as to question the agency of the memories of convicts, a historically subjugated group.

title: The Effect of Rheological Lubricant Properties on Manufacturing Process of Thin-Walled CuBe2 Alloy Tubes
abstract: In the manufacturing process of high-precision thin-walled tubes with diameters of less than 3 mm, the deformation conditions at the contact area between the die, the tube and the floating plug are the decisive factor in the stability of the drawing process. These conditions depend, amongst other things, on the rheological properties of the lubricants, temperature and friction conditions. Industrial drawing trials of ultra-thin beryllium bronze tubes have demonstrated a correlation between the physico-chemical properties of the lubricants and the susceptibility of the tubes to breakage, as well as the efficiency of the drawing process. The maximum drawing speed that guarantees stable process conditions depends on the dynamic viscosity coefficient, the thermal stability of the lubricant, the drawing force, the temperature and the amount of lubricant on the tube surface. As the tube drawing speed increases, the temperature at the material/tool interface rises. This leads to a gradual decrease in the viscosity of the lubricants, a reduction in the thickness of the lubricant film, and an increase in friction, drawing force and the strength properties of the tubes. Once the critical speed is exceeded, the tube breaks in the drawing die. title: Research Progress on Additives for Lubricating Oils and Greases: From Conventional Functional Additives to Multidimensional Nanomaterials
abstract: Lubricating oils and greases constitute an indispensable tribological assurance system spanning automotive, industrial, aerospace, and emerging energy sectors. The performance of lubricants fundamentally depends on the synergistic interplay between base oils, thickeners (for greases), and a diverse portfolio of functional additives. This review systematically summarizes the research progress in lubricant additives, with emphasis on both conventional functional additives and emerging nanomaterial-based additives. For conventional additives, we examine the mechanisms, evolution, and interfacial interactions of anti-wear agents (exemplified by zinc dialkyldithiophosphate and organomolybdenum compounds), friction modifiers (including organic friction modifiers and functionalized polymers), dispersants, and viscosity index improvers. Particular attention is devoted to the synergistic and antagonistic effects arising from additive combinations. Subsequently, we comprehensively review the development of nanomaterial additives through a dimensional engineering lens—zero-dimensional (0D) nanoparticles, one-dimensional (1D) nanotubes/nanowires, two-dimensional (2D) layered materials, three-dimensional (3D) hierarchical architectures, and critically, multidimensional hybrid systems. title: Insurers’ Investments and Insurance Prices
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences
abstract: We develop a theory in which stable funding from insurance underwriting allows insurers to earn the liquidity premium on illiquid assets and pass part of it back to policyholders through lower prices. Consistent with the model’s predictions, we show empirically that (1) insurance prices are lower when the liquidity premium is higher, for both life insurers and property and casualty insurers. (2) In the cross-section, insurers with more stable funding earn higher expected returns and set lower prices. (3) It is specifically the part of expected returns driven by stable funding that passes through to prices. The findings highlight the value of insurance underwriting as a stable source of funding, with benefits that flow back to policyholders. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. title: Fatigue crack growth without plasticity under cyclically reversed shear
abstract: We show that cyclic fatigue can occur in a system whose elements behave elastically up to an irreversible failure threshold, without plasticity, friction, or any time-dependent process. The model represents a weak interface between two elastic bodies loaded in shear. Under sufficiently large cyclic loading below the static failure threshold, a pre-existing flaw advances progressively, by a few lattice spacings per cycle. Two conditions are needed for this behavior: each bond fails more easily under one sense of the shear than the opposite, and the shear must be reversed during the cycle by an amount large enough to break bonds that have not yet failed. The model thus identifies the minimal conditions for an intrinsic, plasticity-free fatigue mechanism. Such conditions may be met at interfaces and weak planes subjected to strongly reversed shear, as in fretting, rolling contact, and reversed torsion, or in cyclic shear of cemented granular materials.

title: Collision Response Analysis of a Suspended Rubber-Tube Height-Restriction Warning Frame Subjected to Overheight Vehicle Impact Using LS-DYNA
abstract: Traditional height-limiting warning barriers address the issues of susceptibility to damage and difficulty in operation and maintenance. This paper proposes a rubber-tube-suspended height-restriction frame. Based on the LSDYNA explicit dynamics platform, a finite element model for an over-height vehicle height-restriction frame was developed to simulate collisions between over-height vehicles and the rubber-tube height-restriction frame. The model systematically analyzes the collision response patterns under full-width frontal collisions and lateral collisions with offsets of 1/2 and 1/4. The results indicate that a frontal collision consists of two concentrated contact phases: an initial high-intensity impact followed by a secondary low-intensity impact. During these phases, the maximum contact reaction force reaches 148.3 kN, providing effective tactile feedback for the driver without damaging the vehicle’s roof steel structure. The secondary impact occurs during the phase where the vehicle and the rubber tube move in the same direction, at which point the peak contact force drops to 35 kN. This energy dissipation is attributed to the combined effect of reduced relative velocity at the contact interface and the unloading of tangential slip. title: Research Progress on the Tribological Properties of Porous Oil-Impregnated Polyimide for Bearing Cages
abstract: Abstract Porous oil-impregnated polyimide (iPPI) combines the functions of oil storage, oil supply, and oil reabsorption, offering significant potential for applications in space bearings and under starved-oil lubrication applications. This Review focuses on research progress in the tribological properties of porous polyimide (PPI), systematically elaborating on its structural characteristics, liquid storage behavior, self-lubricating antiwear mechanisms, and performance optimization methods. The formation mechanism, the structural characteristics, and their impact on the oil and mechanical properties of pores are highlighted. Research progress in lubrication models, friction-contact types, PPI modification, structural optimization, preparation technology optimization, and lubricant medium optimization is summarized. The results indicate that the tribological properties of iPPI are determined by the pore structure, the properties of the lubricating medium, and its dynamic migration behavior within the pores and are significantly influenced by the service conditions and the counterpart materials. Research in this field is progressively shifting from single-parameter adjustment toward collaborative design and predictable design for complex service requirements.

title: The Sovereign Soul
abstract: This chapter asks how courts and constitutions can protect the sovereign soul, understood as the interior space of thought, feeling, and choice, in a world where synthetic cognition becomes cheaper and more capable than human reasoning (Ienca & Andorno, 2017; Farahany, 2023). title: Biomimetic 4D Printing via Poisson Contraction Theory: From Layer-by-Layer Deposition to Boundary-Programmed Poroelastic Self-Assembly
abstract: Additive manufacturing and 4D printing enable complex soft structures, but the fabrication of continuous anisotropic membranes, embedded functional paths, and independently gliding interfaces remains challenging. This perspective explores a complementary strategy inspired by Poisson Contraction Theory (PCT): a mechanobiological hypothesis in which boundary-constrained tensile deformation promotes transverse contraction and fiber reorientation in fibrous, fluid-saturated materials. abstract: Abstract Buried rigid conduits in trench installations are commonly protected by exploiting positive soil arching, which reduces the vertical stress transmitted to the conduit crown. title: Research on grinding force modeling and surface morphology characteristics evaluation in dry grinding of Ti-6Al-4V machined by structured grinding wheel
abstract: Abstract Dry grinding eliminates the use of coolant, reducing environmental pollution and energy consumption, which aligns with the green manufacturing principles of modern industry. However, dry grinding of titanium alloys presents issues such as high grinding forces, surface burning, and increased surface roughness. The design of structured grinding wheels can reduce friction and heat generation during the grinding process, thereby lowering grinding forces and temperatures, which helps to prevent surface burning and cracking resulting in better surface quality. By integrating the curved quadrilateral pyramid grit model, the material properties of titanium alloy TC4, and the surface structural parameters of a regular array structured grinding tool, a theoretical model for grinding force considering instantaneous contact state between the grit and the workpiece has been established. The mapping relationship between grinding forces, surface structural features of grinding tool, and processing parameters was explored. The research findings are of great significance in improving the surface quality of titanium alloy dry grinding with structured tools, enhancing processing efficiency, increasing process stability, promoting environmental protection, and expanding application fields.

abstract: Original simulator-generated dataset accompanying Limits of Sensor-Only Capacity Learning for Safety-Filtered Autonomous Racing: An Auditable Simulation Study by Jose Austin, Ivan Hernando, Jonathan Tanuseputra and Budi Juarto. title: Places
abstract: This chapter reframes Latin America’s oil history through a multiscalar analysis of places, emphasizing how a diversity of sites, from transnational biomes to single oil wells, became both nodes of production and arenas of cultural meaning. Bringing together a wide range of spatial units, this chapter investigates how fossil capitalism transformed environments as diverse as the Amazon, the Chaco, the Bay of All Saints, Maracaibo Lake, national territories, and key urban and extraction centers. Rather than treating these locations as bounded, the chapter conceptualizes them as nodal points in translocal circulations of technology, labor, capital, and expertise. It examines how terrains and ecologies shaped extraction strategies and, in turn, were reshaped by pipelines, ports, refineries, and offshore infrastructures. Simultaneously, it analyzes how states, media, and popular culture inscribed symbolic meanings into these places, linking oil to national identity, modernity, and citizenship. By integrating material and cultural geographies, the chapter illuminates the frictions between infrastructures and inhabitants, the uneven distribution of environmental harm, and the emergence of local resistance. It lays the spatial foundations for understanding how people, machines, and institutions negotiated and contested the making of Latin American oil worlds.

title: Acoustic emission analysis of shear processes in red sandstone with soft red bed interlayers
abstract: Landslides in the red beds are associated with potential slipping along structural planes, which is further aggravated by the presence of weak interlayers within these planes. These weak interlayers, characterized by soft red bed materials with loose structures, play a critical role in the slope slide. However, the precursors to sliding caused by these weak interlayers remain unclear. To address this, the study employed acoustic emission (AE) monitoring—an approach widely recognized for its effectiveness in detecting precursory signals—to investigate potential indicators of slip. AE monitoring was conducted during direct shear tests on red bed interlayers containing soft red rock layers to analyze their behavior prior to slip. The findings reveal that during shearing, the soft red bed in the interlayer first consolidates and then transitions into frictional sliding, resulting in complex and diverse stick-slip events. AE signals show a marked increase in AE activity preceding stick-slip events. Additionally, the friction coefficient increase during shearing is correlated with a decrease in the AE b -value. abstract: Objective This study investigates the micromechanical behaviour of compression wave propagation in granular media using the Discrete Element Method (DEM), with a focus on the evolution and degradation of the oedometric modulus and the damping ratio under harmonic excitation. Methods A C++ DEM model was developed to simulate wave propagation in a granular deposit subjected to base excitation. title: Dialogue as public technology and therefore a demo-technical analysis of participation design
abstract: This thesis explores how the design of public dialogue shapes the democratic and technoscientific dimensions of participation in science and technology governance. Participation is widely promoted within Science and Technology Studies (STS) as one of the main 'solutions' to the 'problems' of politicising technoscience and expanding expertise. In that sense, there is a prevalent conceptualisation in STS that takes a functionalist approach of what participation is for, instead of the more contingent and messy characterisations that STS attributes to technoscience. On this account, there is a gap between the approach STS takes to study technoscience and the approach it takes to study democracy. Addressing this gap, this thesis conceptualises dialogue as a public technology: a culturally embedded, materially mediated, and socio-historically bounded practice in which the 'technical' and the 'democratic' cannot, and should not be separated ex-ante. The research employs a multi-method approach across three comparative strands. First, a critical interpretive review identifies ten design principles for dialogue and the 'design frictions' that emerge when these principles interact, advancing a demo-technical analysis that links normative democratic ideals with technical design decisions. title: CPT-based reliability analysis of offshore monopile foundations using geology-informed hierarchical Bayesian spatial modelling
journal: Georisk Assessment and Management of Risk for Engineered Systems and Geohazards
abstract: Uncertainty in ground conditions strongly influences the reliability of offshore wind monopiles, yet design practice still treats spatial variability, soil stratification and property-transformation uncertainty in isolation. This paper presents an end-to-end Bayesian framework that carries these ground-related uncertainties from cone penetration test (CPT) data through to a monopile serviceability failure probability. A geology-informed hierarchical Gaussian-process regression (HGPR) model produces full posterior predictive distributions of cone resistance in three dimensions, with the soil-unit classification uncertainty entering in the prediction stage through a mixture of per-soil-unit Gaussian Processes. A Bayesian area-wide model then maps cone resistance to the effective friction angle, capturing also the transformation uncertainty, and a tailored conditional Monte Carlo scheme integrates these sources efficiently into the failure probability. Applied to a North Sea offshore wind farm with complex glacial stratigraphy, the framework demonstrates that transformation uncertainty has a large influence on the reliability while vertical spatial variability is largely averaged out along the pile. Loads, pile geometry and material properties are treated deterministically, so the workflow propagates the ground-related uncertainties to structural performance and provides a transparent, practical basis for reliability-based monopile design.

abstract: This paper presents a testing and approval concept for the mechanical safety of photovoltaic (PV) mounting systems on buildings within the European regulatory framework. While IEC module standards ensure electrical and environmental performance, structural safety is governed by Eurocodes and national building regulations, which treat PV substructures as load‑bearing roof or façade components. Documented failures under wind and snow loading underscore the need for building authority approval to demonstrate load‑bearing capacity, standardise documentation, and provide legal certainty for stakeholders. The proposed methodology combines non‑standardised small‑body tests on modular components (module clamps, cross connectors, roof hooks) with complete system tests, particularly for flat‑roof and façade systems. Tailored tensile, shear and compression setups reproduce realistic load paths and installation conditions, including misinstallation scenarios. Characteristic load‑bearing capacities are derived statistically, accounting for scatter due to friction, assembly variability and material overstrength, and are evaluated with respect to serviceability limits as well as ultimate capacity. title: Production Cost Efficiency, Profit Maximization, and Input Substitution in the Manufacturing Industry: A Narrative Review
abstract: Global manufacturing industries face profound structural transformations driven by robotic automation, relative factor-price volatility, rising product-market markups, and stringent decarbonization mandates. abstract: This study investigates a foundational void in the constitutional and legal history of the Korean peninsula: the structural non-existence of political persuasion. In comparative state formation, deliberative persuasion functioned not as moral benevolence, but as a formal transaction cost extorted by the material capacity of direct producers to execute systemic rupture—exemplified by Roman republican plebeian secessions. title: The Embodied Computation Trilemma: Thermodynamic Boundaries, Phase-Space Collapse, and Deterministic Control in Vision-Language-Action Models
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract Contemporary physical artificial intelligence (Physical AI) and vision-language-action (VLA) foundation models rest upon an unproven foundational axiom: that dynamic interaction within continuous physical space-time can be asymptotically resolved by scaling discrete floating-point operations (FLOPs) and multimodal autoregressive tokens. In this work, we formalize the fundamental limits of this paradigm as The Embodied Computation Trilemma, establishing a rigorous mathematical and thermodynamic bound connecting control efficiency ($E$), hardware/compute cost ($C$), and physical safety bounds ($S$): $$\frac{E \cdot S}{C} \le k_{\text{embodied}}$$ Grounded in micro-scale Landauer dissipation and macro-scale second-law thermodynamic constraints, we prove that unconstrained optimization toward maximizing efficiency ($E \to 1$) while stripping away physical safety margins ($S \to 0$) inevitably induces Phase-Space Divergence and Material Constitutive Inadmissibility when confronting discontinuous contact boundaries and friction bifurcations in the real world. To resolve this epistemic deadlock, we introduce a deterministic, zero-heap C99 fault-tolerant state estimator as a zero-stack safety layer, ensuring bounded momentum reacquisition for hard real-time embedded systems. This work bridges abstract algorithmic assets with physical reality, backed by our comprehensive 20-part Physical Intelligence (PI) matrix.

abstract: Abstract Background Product take-back systems are central to circular economy implementation, yet many recoverable products and materials still end up landfilled or downgraded to low-value treatment. abstract: Timely assessment of the condition and key parameters of used engine oil is crucial for preventing sudden mechanical failures, as well as for improving and planning the maintenance of heavy agricultural machinery. This study proposes a non-destructive chemometric method for evaluating the operational condition and additive concentration in oil used for heavy-duty diesel engines. Tribological bench tests are conducted using friction pairs made of various materials (bronze–steel, cast iron–steel, and steel–steel) within a common lubricating medium. Spectral characteristics are obtained in the Vis-NIR range, covering wavelengths from 190 to 992 nm. Due to sensor saturation at wavelengths below 400 nm and above 988 nm, the analysis focused on the 400–988 nm range. Classification and quality assessment models have been developed using Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (PLS-DA) and an artificial neural network (multilayer perceptron – MLP), employing Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV). abstract: Reliable data on soil strength and compressibility are needed for safe and economical foundation design, yet foundations are often designed with little site-specific information. This study characterised the shear strength and settlement behaviour of shallow soils within the University of Ibadan, Southwestern Nigeria, under three land uses: a developed academic area (Zone A), a residential quarters area (Zone B) and an undeveloped area (Zone C). Nine samples were taken at depths of 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 m and tested for particle size distribution, natural moisture content, standard Proctor compaction, direct shear and one-dimensional consolidation to BS 1377. abstract: The effect of nominal TiB 2 additions (0 to 30 vol pct) on the microstructure, hardness, sliding wear, and solid-particle erosion resistance of arc-melted Al 0.7 CoCrFeNiTi 0.2 high-entropy alloy was investigated. X-ray diffraction showed a predominantly FCC matrix with a minor BCC/B2 contribution, while distinct TiB 2 reflections were observed only for the 30 vol pct material. SEM–EDS revealed increasingly pronounced Ti- and B-rich segregation with increasing TiB 2 addition and coarse plate-like TiB 2 particles at 30 vol pct. Hardness increased from 457 HV 5 for the reference alloy to a maximum of 663 HV 5 at 15 vol pct TiB 2 , then decreased to 574 HV 5 at 30 vol pct. Sliding wear resistance improved markedly up to 15 vol pct TiB 2 , for which the specific wear rate decreased by approximately 82 pct and the coefficient of friction reached its minimum. In contrast, the best solid-particle erosion resistance at 90 deg impingement was obtained at 5 vol pct TiB 2 , with approximately 38 pct lower volume loss than the reference alloy. Higher nominal TiB 2 additions increased erosion loss despite higher hardness. The results demonstrate that the nominal TiB 2 addition providing the best performance among the investigated compositions depends on the degradation mechanism and is governed by the combined effects of matrix strengthening, reinforcement morphology, microstructural heterogeneity, and impact- or sliding-induced damage.

abstract: This dissertation investigates the dynamics of current-driven magnetic skyrmions, topological solitons in magnetic materials with broken spatial inversion symmetry, for low-power spintronic applications like racetrack memory and multilevel data storage. Skyrmions’ small size and low driving current requirements make them promising information carriers. The research examines skyrmion motion under driving currents, pinning effects, and thermal fluctuations, using numerical simulations (Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation), analytical studies (Thiele equation), and theoretical modeling to design novel data storage devices. The skyrmion Hall angle, influenced by current and pinning, provides insights for ambient-condition devices. title: Analysis of Aero-drag System in Cars for Efficient Braking
abstract: This work explores integrating aerodynamic forces with traditional braking systems to improve braking efficiency and shorten the stopping distances. Although, conventional brakes use friction, a vehicle's deceleration can be greatly increased by taking advantage of air resistance. There is a major role of aerodynamic drag forces in the handling of an aircraft the concept of which has been utilized here to perform the braking requirements in a car. By using an extra fitment in the vehicle body such as a rear wing can lead to this similar behavior of the increased air drag resistance. Similar wings can be seen in the modern-day sports car which have active air drag increasing and drag reduction systems are capable of providing better handling with help of air drag. The goal of the research is to analyse the effects of aerodynamic forces acting on the vehicle body. Braking distances has been calculated both with and without the effect of aerodynamic forces. Also, by the help of simulation tool the performance of the wing has been analysed. The results indicate significant effect of rear wing angle over aerodynamic drag resistance.

journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part D Journal of Automobile Engineering
abstract: Traditional tire mechanism models often fail to accurately capture the complex dynamic characteristics of the tire-road interface, whereas purely data-driven models suffer from insufficient physical consistency. To address these issues, this paper proposes a data-driven physics-informed adaptive weighted fusion (DP-AWF) method for modeling tire longitudinal force-slip characteristics. The proposed method first employs a wavelet-function-enhanced Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) to learn the nonlinear mapping among slip ratio, vertical load, and longitudinal force. title: A Safe-Load Bound for Cargo Behind the Rear Axle of a Small Motorcycle on Unpaved Roads
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Small motorcycles of the 125 cc class carry much of the light freight on unpaved roads in many regions, frequently with cargo stacked on a rack behind the rear axle at loads of 100 kg or more. This paper computes the safe-load bound for such cargo from three limits evaluated together: the front-wheel load fraction, braking distance, and the rear tyre load rating. The reference machine weighs 110 kg with a 75 kg rider (185 kg combined, wheelbase 1.30 m, front wheel carrying 41.5% unladen), and the cargo centre is 0.60 m behind the rear axle. Requiring the front wheel to retain at least 25% of the total weight for steering gives a maximum cargo load of 42.8 kg. The rear tyre rating (load index 54, 212 kg) permits 71.0 kg, so steering, not the tyre, sets the bound; with a 10% tyre margin the tyre limit falls to 56.5 kg, still above the steering bound. Braking from 40 km/h on dirt takes 12.6–21.0 m of braking distance at friction coefficients of 0.50–0.30, plus 11.1 m of reaction distance. Loads of the size commonly observed are outside every limit at once: at 100 kg of cargo the front wheel carries 10.7% of the weight and the rear tyre is at 120.0% of its rating; at 150 kg the front wheel carries 2.2% — 7.5 kg in total — and the rear tyre is at 154.5% of its rating. The bound is 42.8 kg at 0.60 m behind the axle, rising to 54.7 kg if the load is moved forward to 0.40 m behind the axle and falling to 35.2 kg at 0.80 m.

journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Heuristic Optimization of Study Schedules Based on Cognitive and Chronobiological Load
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Inadequate time management among students often overlooks the physiological and cognitive constraints of human learning, leading to sleep deprivation, metabolic dysregulation, and working memory overload. While traditional planners operate as static schedules that assume an infinite energy reserve, the omission of nighttime rest, regular nutrition, and physical recovery compromises the consolidation of information into long-term memory and increases the risk of academic burnout. To address this issue, this article proposes CL-CHRONOS (Cognitive-Load & Chronobiological Heuristic Resource Optimization Network Operating Scheduler), a four-layer algorithmic model for academic scheduling. Unlike most academic scheduling models that optimize only available physical time, CL-CHRONOS explicitly incorporates cognitive energy as a constrained resource within the allocation process.
