title: A Gravity Ropeway for Hillside Produce: Sizing, Throughput, and the Drop Below Which Gravity Drive Fails
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A gravity ropeway moves produce down a hillside with no engine: a loaded carrier descending pulls an empty carrier back up. This paper sizes such a system and derives the condition under which it runs at all. The baseline design — a 400 m horizontal span with a 60 m elevation drop, 12 mm steel wire rope, a 60 kg carrier carrying 200 kg of produce — develops a driving force of 291 N against 228 N of friction and fixed losses, leaving a net force of only 63 N. At a controlled descent speed of 2.0 m/s with 90 s of loading and unloading per cycle, it delivers 2,464 kg/hour, or about 19,700 kg in an 8-hour day, and the lower-station brake must dissipate 25.7 kJ per cycle (0.13 kW mean during descent). Maximum wire tension at a design sag of 10.0 m is 36.21 kN, a safety factor of only 2.21 against an 80 kN breaking load — below good practice, so a heavier rope is required in any real build. Self-running requires a drop-to-span ratio of at least 0.117: minimum drops are 46.8 m at a 400 m span, 35.1 m at 300 m, and 70.2 m at 600 m. Below that ratio — for example, a 400 m span with a 40 m drop, or any payload below about 150 kg on the baseline span — gravity drive fails and a powered drive is required. That failure map, not the headline throughput, is the design's most important output.

title: Pedestrian Death Physics: A Survivable Speed Bound for Crossings from Stopping Distance, Fatality Risk, and Available Sight Distance
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: SIMULATED, NOT MEASURED. A pedestrian crossing is survivable at a given traffic speed only if a driver who first sees the pedestrian at the available sight distance can stop before reaching them, or can shed enough speed that a strike is unlikely to be fatal. Combining stopping-distance kinematics (reaction plus braking), a logistic fatality-risk curve for struck pedestrians, and available sight distance at crossings, this paper derives a design table mapping sight distance to the maximum traffic speed at which a full stop is still possible. On a wet surface (friction coefficient 0.40) with a 1.5 s reaction time, 10 m of sight distance supports only 17.1 km/h, 20 m supports 28.6 km/h, 30 m supports 38.0 km/h, and 50 m supports 53.2 km/h; with a conservative 2.5 s design reaction time the caps fall to 12.3 km/h at 10 m and 22.0 km/h at 20 m. The risk curve places a 10% fatality risk at an impact speed of 25.9 km/h and a 52.4% risk at 50 km/h; wet stopping distance at 50 km/h is 45.4 m. Under the stated sight-triangle geometry (ratio 2.33), clearing an obstruction back 6 m buys 14.0 m of sight distance, and holding 30 km/h on a wet surface requires about 9.1 m of clearing, while 50 km/h requires 19.5 m. Two regimes defeat the bound: approaches occluded to 5 m, where the survivable cap is 9.8 km/h wet and 10.5 km/h dry, below any normal traffic speed; and wet high-speed arterials, where stopping from 80 km/h needs 96.3 m and a strike at that speed carries a 0.950 fatality risk.

abstract: Abstract Stationary diesel engines remain important for agricultural, industrial, and power‐generation applications, yet limited emission‐control technologies can lead to elevated pollutant emissions and environmental burdens. title: Optimisation of Performance and Emissions of a SI Engine Operated with H 2 -Gasohol E20 Blends Using Response Surface Methodology
abstract: This study investigates the application of hydrogen (H2) as a combustion enhancer in sparkignition engines for the purpose of decarbonization. It assesses the impact of hydrogen energy fraction (HEF, 10–20%) and engine load (EL, 2–6 bar IMEP) on the combustion, performance, and emissions of a gasoline direct injection engine (GDI). Gasohol E20 was utilized as the primary direct-injected fuel, with H2 introduced via port injection. The experiments were structured using a Central Composite Design (CCD) within a Response Surface Methodology (RSM) framework to model brake thermal efficiency (BTE), brake-specific fuel consumption (BSFC), CO 2 , and NOx emissions. An increase in H 2 content resulted in enhanced in-cylinder and peak cylinder pressures compared to those of E20. The highest BTE of48.94% was achieved at 15% HEF and 4 bar EL, representing a 29.3% improvement over the baseline. The lowest BSFC recorded was 230.16 g/kWh, indicating a 34.9% reduction. CO 2 emissions decreased by up to 15.8% at 20% HEF and 6 bar EL, although there was an increase in thermal NOx emissions, peaking at 2251 ppm. Multi-objective optimization identified 17.7% HEF and 3.5 bar EL as optimal conditions (BTE = 43.32%, BSFC = 275.70 g/kWh, CO 2 = 11.67 %vol, NOx = 1958.77 ppm). Validation with 1D AVL CRUISE M simulation demonstrated prediction errors below 3.7%, confirming the RSM-CCD framework as a reliable calibration tool for H 2 /E20 dual-fuel GDI engines.

title: Modelling and Validation of Performance Characteristics and Emission Reduction in GDI Engine using Port Water Injection
abstract: Environmental regulations necessitate reductions in pollutants and greenhouse gas emissions from internal combustion engines. While downsized gasoline direct injection (GDI) engines improve thermal efficiency, they remain constrained by end-gas autoignition (knocking) and produce elevated nitrogen oxides (NOx). This manuscript investigates the impact of port water injection (PWI) on the combustion, performance, and emission characteristics of a GDI engine fuelled with gasohol E20 under steady-state cruising conditions. A 1D numerical simulation was developed using AVL Cruise M and validated against experimental data, evaluating water-to-fuel (W/F) mass ratios up to 30%. Results demonstrate that introducing 30% water completely suppresses knocking, allowing spark-ignition timing optimisation to recover brake thermal efficiency. The combined effects of water's high latent heat and dilution yield up to 80% reduction in engine-out NOx emissions. Additionally, the findings validate PWI as an effective thermodynamic intervention to mitigate knocking, NOx, and other emissions without requiring aftertreatment.

title: Optimization, fuel characterization, and variable compression ratio diesel engine performance and emission of biodiesel from three different nonedible seed oils
abstract: Abstract The present study investigates the engine compatibility of biodiesel derived from three non‐edible second‐generation feedstocks, Gossypium hirsutum (GHO), Hevea brasiliensis (HBO), and Pongamia pinnata (PPO), under identical operating conditions. title: Double-pulse diesel injection strategy on combustion performance and emission characteristics of turbocharged multi-cylinder CRDI dual-fuel diesel engine fueled with gasoline/diesel and ethanol/diesel
abstract: Rising environmental regulations and increasing fossil fuel costs have intensified the search for sustainable and renewable fuel alternatives. abstract: Heavy-duty diesel engines significantly contribute to environmental degradation, motivating the search for sustainable alternatives like plant-derived biodiesel. This study investigates the performance and emissions of a novel ternary hybrid biodiesel blend made from shea butter, neem oil, and waste kitchen oils (40.41:19.73:39.86 w/w) in a direct-injection, four-stroke, single-cylinder diesel engine. Various fuel blends (B0, B10, B20, B30, B40, B100) were evaluated against conventional diesel. The experimental results show that all tested biodiesel blends exhibit consistently shorter ignition delays than diesel due to higher cetane numbers (57 for B100 versus 52 for B0). At full load, biodiesel blends reduced carbon monoxide and hydrocarbon emissions by up to 26.79% and 41.06%, respectively. abstract: Abstract In this study, biodiesel (AKOME) produced from apricot kernel oil through the transesterification method was blended with diesel fuel in volumetric ratios of 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20% (B5, B10, B15, B20). Based on 60 experimental observations (3 repetitions × 4 speeds × 5 blends), the Response Surface Methodology (RSM) models exhibited high prediction accuracy, ranging from R2 = 0.890 (CO) to R2 = 0.976 (BSFC). Sufficient Precision values remained well above the recommended minimum threshold of 4.0 for all response variables (34.98–67.96). title: Performance of a Four-Stroke Diesel Engine Using LPG
abstract: This study investigates the performance and emission characteristics of a single-cylinder, four-stroke, water-cooled diesel engine operated in dual-fuel mode using Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) and diesel. A vaporized LPG system with regulators, mixers, and safety controls was integrated into the air intake while diesel served as the pilot fuel. Experiments were conducted under varying loads and LPG substitution ratios. Key parameters measured include brake thermal efficiency (BTE), brake specific fuel consumption (BSFC), exhaust gas temperature (EGT), and emissions (CO, HC, NOₓ). Results showed up to a 12% improvement in BTE at part load and significant reductions in CO and smoke, although NOₓ emissions increased due to higher combustion temperatures. Performance declined at high LPG ratios due to lean mixtures. The findings support LPG as a viable alternative fuel in CI engines with potential for further optimization through fuel control and injection timing.

title: Influence of Fuel Injection Pressure on Gasoline/Waste Oil Biodiesel–diesel Blend (B20) RCCI Combustion: An Experimental Study
abstract: Waste oil-derived biodiesel is a promising renewable fuel for advanced combustion concepts such as Reactivity Controlled Compression Ignition (RCCI). However, the influence of fuel injection pressure (FIP) on gasoline/biodiesel RCCI combustion has received limited experimental attention. In this study, the effect of FIP was experimentally investigated using a diesel–waste cooking oil biodiesel blend (B20) as the high-reactivity fuel and gasoline as the low-reactivity fuel. Experiments were conducted at 1050 rpm with a premixed fuel ratio of 27%, over FIPs ranging from 150 to 350 bar and at two start-of-injection (SOI) timings of 25° and 40° bTDC. The study highlights that the response of different engine characteristics to variations in FIP depends on SOI for some parameters, whereas others are largely insensitive to SOI. Engine performance, combustion characteristics, and exhaust emissions were evaluated. The results showed that increasing FIP over a relatively large range increased brake power by up to approximately 2.4 times the minimum value, whereas the in-cylinder pressure peak did not follow the same trend. In addition, among the FIPs associated with relatively high brake power, an FIP was identified that resulted in lower NOx emissions at both SOIs while providing the highest brake power at one SOI. These findings demonstrate the importance of considering both FIP and SOI when selecting injection conditions for gasoline/B20 RCCI combustion.

title: Sustainability-oriented experimental and GRA–ANOVA optimization of ethyl acetate/ n -butanol/nitromethane gasoline blends in a spark-ignition engine
journal: Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers Part E Journal of Process Mechanical Engineering
abstract: This study experimentally investigated and optimized the effects of gasoline blends containing ethyl acetate, n -butanol, and nitromethane on the performance, exhaust emissions, noise, and vibration behavior of a single-cylinder spark-ignition engine. A sustainability-oriented multi-domain optimization framework was employed to quantify trade-offs among fuel economy, performance, emissions, and noise–vibration responses and assess optimum robustness. Experiments were conducted using pure gasoline and 12 gasoline-based blends under full-throttle conditions at 1200–2800 r/min. Fuel effects depended strongly on engine speed and blend composition. At 2000 r/min, G97EA1NB1NM1 reduced brake-specific fuel consumption by 9.49%, while G94EA6 reduced brake-specific energy consumption by 12.42% and increased thermal efficiency by 13.52%. At 2400 r/min, G94NB3NM3 reduced CO by 58.33%, while G97NB1.5NM1.5 reduced hydrocarbons by 23.65%. G94EA3NB3 achieved the greatest NO x reduction (74.10%) at 2800 r/min, although some nitromethane-containing blends substantially increased NO x . Noise changes remained limited, whereas G94EA3NB3 reduced vibration by 16.60% at 2800 r/min. Gray relational analysis identified G94EA3NM3–1600 r/min as the overall and performance-based optimum and G94EA3NB3–2800 r/min as the emission and noise–vibration-based optimum. title: Smart biodiesel systems in integrating nano-additives and artificial intelligence for cleaner internal combustion engines
abstract: The transition toward sustainable transport and energy systems requires integrated innovations that address both technical performance and environmental sustainability. This review examines the synergistic roles of biodiesel, nano additives, and artificial intelligence as enablers of clean energy adoption. Biodiesel derived from first- to fourth-generation feedstocks offers a renewable alternative to fossil diesel, with life cycle assessments reporting reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, improved air quality, and comparable engine efficiency. Biodiesel-nano-additive system improvements reportedly yield approximately 3-10% improvement in brake thermal efficiency and up to 12% reduction in brake-specific fuel consumption, along with lower particulate matter, carbon monoxide, and hydrocarbon emissions under optimum operating conditions. AI-based optimization techniques make it possible to forecast fuel properties, combustion characteristics, and engine performance in biodiesel-fueled systems. Beyond technological performance, this review highlights environmental, economic, and policy implications of integrating these domains. title: Energy Modeling and Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Capacity Sizing for Diesel-to-Battery Rail Retrofitting
abstract: Decarbonizing the transportation sector requires practical pathways for reducing fossil-fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions from existing rail systems. Although railway electrification through catenary systems offers an effective pathway toward low-emission rail transportation, its widespread implementation on existing non-electrified corridors can be constrained by substantial capital costs, infrastructure modifications, and deployment complexity. Battery-electric and battery-supported locomotive technologies provide an alternative pathway for rail decarbonization by enabling progressive fleet electrification while reducing dependence on extensive wayside electrical infrastructure. This study presents a route-level energy assessment to determine the onboard battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity required to retrofit an F59PH diesel passenger locomotive for battery-electric operation on the Piedmont corridor. The journey is simulated using the Single Train Simulator (STS), incorporating route characteristics, speed restrictions, station stops, and vehicle configuration. The resulting traction-energy demand provides the basis for evaluating commercially available battery technologies under battery-only and hybrid battery-supported operating scenarios. title: The Influence of Ammonia Port Injection on Combustion Dynamics and Particulate Matter Properties in a Gasoline Direct Injection Engine
abstract: Ammonia (NH 3 ) is a promising zero-carbon fuel for decarbonising transport, although its low reactivity limits its direct use. This study investigated the combustion and emission characteristics of an NH 3 -gasoline dual-fuel high-compression gasoline direct injection (GDI) engine. Gaseous NH 3 was port-injected up to a 30% energy ratio (AER), with gasoline direct-injected as a high-reactivity combustion promoter. Testing across various indicated loads revealed that uncalibrated NH 3 addition severely retarded combustion phasing and suppressed peak cylinder pressures. Applying the maximum brake torque (MBT) spark advance successfully recovered the optimal mass fraction burned phasing and indicated thermal efficiency. However, this necessary calibration exposes a critical emission. Although increasing the AER proportionally reduced engine-out CO 2 and soot particulates, the MBT advance required for combustion stability resulted in higher emissions through thermal and fuel-bound mechanisms. Furthermore, extended late-stage combustion durations indicate a potential unburned NH 3 slip. These findings demonstrate that although NH3 port injection is a viable GDI decarbonisation strategy, dynamic spark calibration is essential. title: Comparative performance evaluation of P2 and P3 hybrid electric vehicle architectures under WLTC driving conditions
abstract: Hybrid Electric Vehicles (HEVs) has drawn considerable attention, aiming as a practical approach to improving fuel economy and lowering vehicle emissions by combining internal combustion engines with electric propulsion systems. Among the various hybrid designs, P2 and P3 configurations stand out for their unique features related to energy transfer, electric driving capability, and overall powertrain performance. This study compares the performance of P2 and P3 HEV architecture using the SimulationX platform under standardized Worldwide Harmonized Light Vehicles Test Cycle (WLTC) conditions. To make a fair comparison focused on hybrid design, both models used the same vehicle specifications, battery parameters, engine and motor performance characteristics, and control inputs. The performance of both architectures was evaluated using key parameters such as fuel mass flow, battery state of charge (SOC), vehicle velocity, and regenerative braking behavior. The results show that both architectures effectively use electric mode during low-speed conditions below 40 km/h, which reduces fuel consumption during urban driving. title: Combustion control strategies to achieve low temperature combustion in PCCI engines - A comprehensive review
abstract: Low-temperature combustion (LTC) has emerged as a pivotal solution for modern compression ignition engines, effectively breaking the traditional nitrogen oxide (NOx) and soot emission trade-off. Among LTC variants, Premixed Charge Compression Ignition (PCCI) stands out for its capacity to reduce in-cylinder emissions with minimal structural modifications. This review evaluates alternative fuel integration within PCCI regimes by shifting from isolated, single-variable engine tuning to a unified multi-parameter coupling framework. abstract: Low-cost smartphone telematics can support transparent trip-level profiling in road freight operations, but telemetry-derived labels require careful interpretation. We analyse an extract of 52 freight trips by 12 drivers (11,434.91 km) associated with a platform reporting 753,021 source location records. Distance-normalised acceleration, braking and route-alert indicators were used to construct four rule-based operational tiers (Excellent, Good, Moderate and Poor); K-means was used for exploratory description only. Decision tree (DT), random forest (RF) and k-nearest neighbours were evaluated using a driver-grouped hold-out (37 training and 15 test trips) and leave-one-driver-out cross-validation. In the hold-out, RF achieved accuracies of 0.867 for driving behaviour and 0.933 for the eco-driving proxy. abstract: The pursuit of higher thermal efficiency in next-generation spark-ignition (SI) engines is driving the development of ultra-lean combustion, where intensified flame quenching and knock create new challenges for fuel formulation. title: Angular momentum transport in a newborn protostar--disc system: magnetic braking, spiral arms and the magneto-rotational instability
abstract: Angular momentum transport in young protostar--disc systems involves magnetic braking, magneto-rotational turbulence and gravitational instability, mechanisms that are usually studied separately and on different scales. We present a three-dimensional non-ideal magnetohydrodynamic simulation, including Ohmic and ambipolar diffusion, that follows the collapse of a $1~M_\odot$ dense core continuously from the cloud scale to the formation of the protostar, and then the resulting protostar--disc system for $\sim 64~\mathrm{yr}$ at a resolution of $\sim 10^{-4}~\mathrm{AU}$ at the protostellar surface. We decompose the azimuthally averaged angular momentum budget into Reynolds, Maxwell and gravitational torques, each split into a radial and a meridional component, over a quasi-steady phase of the evolution. title: The Angular Momentum Transfer Budget of the Milky Way Bar from Its Quadrupole Torque
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A bar that rotates through a disc and a halo does not keep its angular momentum. Resonant stars and dark matter particles absorb it, the bar slows, and the disc is rearranged in the process. This paper assembles that exchange into an explicit budget for the Milky Way, starting from published values for the bar's mass and strength and an adopted fraction of the disc that couples strongly at resonance. The bar's quadrupole exerts a tangential force that is a measured fraction of the radial force; multiplying that force scale by the lever arm at corotation gives a specific torque, and dividing the specific angular momentum at corotation by that torque gives the exchange timescale for resonantly coupled material. Combining the timescale with the coupled mass yields the total angular momentum current, which is then compared with the bar's own angular momentum to express the braking rate in fractional terms. The numbers show that the exchange is fast enough to matter over the disc's lifetime but slow enough that the bar observed today is not a transient — a consistency statement that any complete model of the inner Galaxy must reproduce.
